Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty Images View image in fullscreen An Amazon cargo plane after it crashed at Miami international airport on Sunday, in Miami, Florida. Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty Images Florida Amazon cargo plane crashes at Miami airport after it overshoots runway FAA confirms crash as videos show heavy plumes of smoke surrounding aircraft that flew in from Puerto Rico Maya Yang Sun 6 Sep 2026 15.50 EDT First published on Sun 6 Sep 2026 15.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An Amazon cargo plane crashed at Miami international airport in Florida on Sunday afternoon when a flight from Puerto Rico landed and overshot the runway, sending flames and dark smoke into the sky. Videos posted online show heavy plumes of smoke surrounding an aircraft bearing the Amazon arrow logo on its tail. Unconfirmed reports suggest there may be casualties, but details about injuries or fatalities remained unclear. The plane was reported to be flying for Amazon Prime Air. The Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) confirmed the crash in a statement to the Guardian, saying: “21 Air Flight 7598 overran the runway after landing at Miami International Airport around 2 pm local time on Sunday, September 6. The Boeing 767-300 cargo aircraft departed from Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The FAA will investigate.” The plane overran the airport’s diagonal runway and was disabled at the north-west end of the airport, a spokesperson for Miami international airport said. An air and ground stop has been issued at the airport, preventing all other flights from landing or taking off at the busy south Florida hub. “All runways and taxiways at MIA are currently closed as of 3pm and a ground stop is in effect,” the airport said, adding: “Miami-Dade Fire Rescue has responded to the scene.” US transportation secretary Sean Duffy said on X that responders would “assess the scene after an Amazon cargo plane overran the runway”. “If you’re traveling through the area, please expect significant delays and potential cancellations,” he added. The Guardian has also reached out to Amazonand the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) for comment. https://www.politico.eu/article/kazakhst.text: Kazakhstan’s hopes of Eurovision glory next year have hit a bureaucratic wall. The European Broadcasting Union said Thursday that state-owned broadcaster Khabar Agency does not qualify for full membership, after it recently applied to compete in the glitzy annual contest. The EBU said in a statement that Kazakhstan falls outside the European Broadcasting Area, is not a Council of Europe member and lacks formal observer status with the organization. “Khabar Agency therefore does not qualify for full membership at this time.” Advertisement Advertisement Those requirements are set out in the EBU’s statutes , which were relaxed in June to allow broadcasters from some countries outside Europe to become full members. “Khabar Agency is a valued Associate Member of the EBU, and we appreciate its long-standing engagement with the Union,” the statement added. The broadcaster, controlled by Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Culture and Information, took the country to Junior Eurovision five times between 2018 and 2022, finishing as runner-up twice. Associate membership, however, does not provide an automatic route into the senior contest. A small portion of Kazakhstan (albeit an area larger than Greece) lies within geographical Europe, bolstering its claim that it should be able to compete. The EU is the country’s largest trading partner. That said, geography is hardly a deal-breaker. Australia has competed through special invitations since 2015, finishing fourth in May earlier this year. Canada went further this summer: CBC/Radio-Canada became a full EBU member after the rule change and will make its Eurovision debut in 2027. Canada qualifies because it holds observer status with the Council of Europe and meets the EBU’s public-service-media criteria. Russia frequently competed in the past, until it was kicked out of the competition following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, despite most of its vast territory being in Asia. The rejection lands as Eurovision wrestles with another set of geopolitical rules. Five broadcasters boycotted the 2026 contest over the participation of another non-European country, Israel, over its conduct in the Gaza Strip. Dutch broadcaster AVROTROS has already said it will sit out again in 2027. Advertisement Advertisement For now, Kazakhstan remains outside the main contest, with Khabar limited to associate membership. The EBU didn’t respond to POLITICO’s request for comment on Kazakhstan’s potential to compete in the future.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/07/isra.text: Israelis gathered in a moment of silence on Wednesday to mark three years since the Hamas-led attack of 7 October 2023, which a UN inquiry confirmed killed 1,200 people and saw 252 taken hostage.In southern Israel, families mourned at road junctions, bomb shelters and the site of the Nova music festival, all places overrun by militants in the deadliest attack against Israel.It is the first anniversary on which all the hostages that survived have returned home, bringing a new phase of mourning.Among those marking the day was Elkana Bohbot, 37, who was abducted from the Nova festival and is spending the anniversary in Israel for the first time. He was freed last year after 738 days in captivity, most of it in a tunnel 50 metres underground. He said his daughter's birth in August this year was a message to his captors that "we [Israelis] were here, and we will always be here forever".At the site of the Nova music festival, where Hamas militants in trucks and paragliders opened fire around dawn on October 7, family members bowed their heads in silence, although AFP reported at least one put on techno music in tribute to the fallen.European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen paid her respects to the victims and their families in a post on X."The unspeakable savagery and terror of 7 October must never happen again," she wrote."The EU remains ready to help turn today's fragile ceasefire into a durable peace, based on a two-state solution."The ceasefire von der Leyen referred to took effect last October, two years into the war Israel launched against Hamas in response to the attack.Up to 75,000 Palestinians have been killed in the retaliatory campaign, according to the UN.The UN said this summer that about 1.7 million Palestinians, roughly 80% of the population, were living in tents and temporary accommodation while Israeli maps show more than half of the Gaza strip is now controlled by its troops.On Wednesday, AFP reporters in Israel heard loud bangs from across the border in Gaza during the commemorations as Israel carried out new strikes, despite the ceasefire agreement.Gaza officials said at least two people were killed in overnight strikes in the region, most of which has been reduced to rubble.Wednesday's gatherings were separate from the government's official memorial services, held on 5 October to fall closer to the anniversary in the Hebrew calendar.Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed there would be "no forgiveness for the murderers" and promised never to allow Hamas to rule in Gaza.More than 200 former hostages and relatives wrote to Netanyahu last year demanding an inquiry into the 7 October attacks or his resignation but Israel's leader opted to publish redacted government documents instead of launching an investigation and described the attacks as "a serious intelligence failure".An election follows at the end of the month.

Photograph: Daniel Munoz/Reuters View image in fullscreen Sydney’s Villawood immigration detention centre, where eight fires were reported to have been lit between February and May. Photograph: Daniel Munoz/Reuters Australian immigration and asylum New spate of stabbings, overdoses and fires at Australian immigration detention centres run by ICE-linked US prison firm Exclusive: Federal government under scrutiny as documents reveal serious security lapses at Melbourne and Villawood immigration detention centres Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Christopher Knaus and Ariel Bogle Fri 9 Oct 2026 10.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 17.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A new spate of stabbings, overdoses and drug use in Australia’s immigration detention centres has put the Australian government in likely breach of laws designed to protect staff and detainees, internal documents show. Earlier this year, Guardian Australia revealed catastrophic security failings across Australia’s onshore immigration network since Management and Training Corporation – a US private prison company used by Donald Trump to hold ICE detainees – won the $2.3bn detention contract in late 2024. The federal government has repeatedly attempted to take a stick to MTC and its local subsidiary Secure Journeys to improve its performance, including through financial penalties and a fiery meeting last year between the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, and the company’s global president. Escapes, fires, stabbing: catastrophic security failures revealed in Australia’s immigration detention network Read more But new documents seen by the Guardian show serious security lapses have continued since, including through a spate of eight fire-related incidents at Villawood immigration detention centre and violence and drug use at Melbourne immigration detention centre (MIDC). Those failings have again put the department itself in the crosshairs of Comcare, the federal work safety regulator. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The documents reveal a string of incidents at MIDC involving violence, aggression, illicit substances and improvised weaponry since August. That includes a violent altercation on 18 August between two groups that led to six detainees being hospitalised for “slashing and stabbing injuries made using improvised weapons”. On 10 September, a detainee was found overdosed in his room, requiring staff to administer Naloxone, a drug that reverses opioid overdose effects. The incidents at MIDC prompted Comcare to warn the government that it was failing to control the rising number of “incidents of this type at MIDC and across the broader immigration detention network”. That failure meant it was likely to be in breach of the law, the document said. “I have formed the reasonable belief that the department is contravening section 19 of the WHS Act by failing to ensure, so far as is reasonably practicable, the health and safety of workers and other persons,” Comcare said in its notice. “In particular, the risks associated with violence, aggression, and the presence of illicit substances and improvised weaponry are not being adequately managed. “While the department has advised that a range of actions have been undertaken to address these risks, it has not sufficiently demonstrated that the control measures currently in place are effective in eliminating or minimising the risks, so far as is reasonably practicable.” Comcare said the information available indicates these hazards pose an ongoing risk of serious harm to workers and others in the centres. A separate Comcare document revealed that a series of eight fire-related incidents had taken place at Villawood immigration detention centre between February and May. View image in fullscreen Fire damage to a room at Villawood That’s despite prior warnings to government to intervene after previous fires lit inside Villawood exposed serious gaps in MTC’s preparedness. That includes one fire on 23 September 2025, when MTC staff rushed into a detainee’s room to save him from a fire without proper safety equipment, causing two workers to be hospitalised. The regulator found the department had not conducted its own systematic review of “all fire and smoke control measures falling within its influence or control”, a likely breach of work health and safety regulations. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “The occurrence of multiple notifiable fire incidents over a period of approximately four months, particularly after previous regulatory intervention concerning substantially the same risk, provided repeated and compelling circumstances requiring the department to review the effectiveness of relevant control measures,” the Comcare document said. Workers accuse new company managing Australia’s immigration detention centres of running them ‘like a prison’ Read more The Guardian previously revealed a series of incidents across the centres since Secure Journey took over, including escapes, staff injuries and sick detainees missing medical appointments due to a lack of staff to escort them. Lyndal Ryan, national president of the United Workers Union, which represents workers in the centres, said the notices from Comcare show “the continuing dangerous situations facing workers and detainees inside detention centres, and Secure Journeys’ inability or unwillingness to address those issues”. The union has continually raised concerns about understaffing in the centres, and Ryan said Comcare has made it clear that the department has the responsibility to pull Secure Journeys into line. “The list of eight fires at Villawood over a four-month period are signs of the instability and chaos our members are witnessing almost every day,” she said. A spokesperson for MTC’s local subsidiary, Secure Journeys, said: “In response to your questions, I can confirm that Secure Journeys’ commitment to maintaining safe and secure operations, as well as both staff and detainee welfare remains our top priority.” The Australian Border Force was contacted for comment.
